To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Pb-activated outward K current was found in the isolated neurons of Helisoma trivolvis and that the current showed a concentration-dependent activation.

Pb(2+), in concentrations above 1 mM, induces an outwardly directed current in isolated snails neurons, which is non-inactivating, reversibly blocked by Na(1+) and is linear with negative slope in the voltage range between 0 and 60 mV.
The IPb was blocked by tetrodotoxin, but not by tetramethylammonium, suggesting that the IPb is carried by Na-channels, but not by the K-channels.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Pb(2+) induces an increase in the Na(+) conductance of snail neurons.
IPb is a Pb-activated Na-current.
the IPb is not due to a specific Pb-sensitive channel but rather to a non-specific increase in membrane permeability.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Pb(2+), which is a divalent cation with a similar ionic radius as Ca(2+), activates the Na(+) channels of the snail neuron.
the Pb(2+):Ca(2+)-exchange system is not the only mechanism of the Pb-activated current.
IPb is a Na-activated K-current, which is induced by Pb-ions and is mediated by a voltage-independent mechanism.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Pb(2+) is a potent activator of Na+ currents in snail neurons and the IPb is mediated by the activation of Na+ channels.
Pb(2+) can be an effective activator of the Na channel.
Pb-activated current is not a single channel current but a composite of several types of channels.
